newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO talks grind on, readiness in Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO talks grind on, readiness in Hebron.

text.p: Preparations for Israel's transfer of the volatile town of Hebron to PLO rule are proceeding as negotiators struggle to put the deal on paper.

Late on Wednesday, hundreds of Israeli troops who have gathered in the heart of Hebron where some 400 Jews live and study amidst the town's 100,000 Palestinians staged a large- scale exercise, Palestinian witnesses and Israeli media said.

Entrances to Hebron were closed and ambulances and army vehicles sped back and forth. In an ominous note for the town that has long been a flashpoint of violence, Israel television said troops drilled evacuating wounded.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Wednesday cancelled a trip to the United States only hours before he was to leave in hopes the sides might be close to a deal.
"The prime minister decided to stay in the country in order to help to further the negotiations which are at a sensitive stage," a statement issued by Netanyahu's office said.
Asked if a deal might be clinched on Wednesday night, an Israeli official who spoke on condition he not be named said: "It's possible but it's also possible it will happen tomorrow."
Negotiators met into the early hours of Thursday at U.S. Ambassador to Israel Martin Indyk's home near Tel Aviv.
The sides have been trying for more than a month to close the deal under which Israeli troops would hand over 80 percent of Hebron to Palestinian police.
Two Palestinian negotiators met Netanyahu in Tel Aviv on Wednesday night before heading for Indyk's residence.
"We met with Mr Netanyahu and we discussed all issues in general without getting into the details," top Palestinian negotiator Mahmoud Abbas, also known as Abu Mazen, told Reuters.
Palestinian sources said the Netanyahu meeting came after PLO negotiators earlier met Israeli President Ezer Weizman.

Israel has completed many of the security arrangements for the transfer of the bulk of the city to Palestinian police. But all of the Jews and 15,000 to 20,000 Arabs will remain in the heart of the city under Israeli control, military sources say.

Palestinian officials said after an earlier round of talks on Wednesday that the sides were in stalemate over Israel's demand that its forces be allowed to enter Palestinian- controlled parts of Hebron in "hot pursuit" of suspected attackers.
The Palestinians also are pushing that the accord include an Israeli commitment to carry out further redeployments in West Bank rural areas promised by the previous Israeli government.
Israeli spokesman Moshe Fogel said the sides had achieved "significant progress" and were trying to define how Israeli forces might operate against "terrorists" in PLO-run areas.

Netanyahu, who in May elections ousted the centre-left government that signed the Hebron deal with the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) a year ago, wants to modify the accord to increase security measures for Jewish settlers.
The Hebron pullout was due last March but was delayed after Moslem militant suicide bomb attacks in Israel.
Jews in Hebron on Wednesday warned of bloodshed if Netanyahu carried out the Hebron redeployment.
"What we say today is that there is a potential massacre and pogrom again in Hebron," settler Noam Arnon said, recalling the slaughter by Arabs in 1929 of some 60 Jews in Hebron.
Palestinians in Hebron have the same fear of the Jews. U.S.-born Baruch Goldstein, a Jew from the adjacent Kiryat Arba settlement, massacred 29 Palestinians in Hebron in 1994.
An Israeli military source briefing reporters said tensions in the city were high, adding: "I see so many problems in Hebron, it's a very tough neighbourhood."
